overview: Gojoseon, or Old Joseon, was an early state associated with Liaodong and the northwestern Korean Peninsula. The imported 400-323 BCE dates cover only part of its history. This map’s enormous outline extends far beyond that historical focus and should not be read as an established frontier. Its beginnings and early centres remain debated.

periods.summary: Later accounts describe growing royal authority and rivalry with Yan.

periods.title: Changing frontiers
periods.summary: Yan attacked in the early third century BCE; the kingdom’s territory and political circumstances changed.

periods.title: Later Wiman Joseon
periods.summary: Wiman’s ruling house controlled a powerful trading state before Han conquest.

sections.title: Kings, diplomacy and a remembered beginning

items.text: A later Chinese account says Joseon’s ruler adopted the title of king as neighbouring Yan also claimed royal status. Historians use this account to trace a major regional power in the late fourth century BCE, while recognizing that its institutions were still developing.

The same account names a minister, Ye, who persuaded the ruler to abandon a planned attack and then negotiated with Yan. This is a glimpse of counsel and diplomacy alongside warfare. The later Yan invasion shows that the resulting peace did not last indefinitely.

The medieval Samguk yusa preserves the founding story of Dangun, born to Hwanung and a bear transformed into a woman. Mugwort, garlic and a test of patience feature in the tale. It is an important story of origins, not an eyewitness record or a recipe for transforming animals.

Table-like dolmen tombs link the Bronze Age landscapes of Liaodong and northwestern Korea. Historian Song Ho Jung interprets their construction as evidence of organized local groups and leaders. Similar burial customs alone cannot reveal the exact boundary of one kingdom.

The broad bronze daggers associated with Gojoseon resemble the outline of a bipa, a stringed instrument. Their blade and handle were made separately and fitted together. The musical nickname describes the shape; this was certainly not an instrument to strum.

A bronze dagger handle attributed to Sincheon preserves a repair. Fresh metal filled a defect, and the surface was polished and its decoration reworked to disguise the join. Even prized metalwork could need mending; the surviving patch lets researchers study the craftsperson’s solution.

At Yeongheung-eup, now Geumya-eup, fragments of a casting mould were found at a dwelling site. A fan-shaped axe also came from the Misong-ri cave. Such northern Bronze Age finds show the practical work behind finished metal objects, although they do not identify a royal workshop.

Bronze did not immediately sweep stone tools away. Archaeologists have found bronze daggers together with polished stone daggers, stone arrowheads and axes. People could use different materials side by side, so the name Bronze Age does not mean every tool was bronze.

Misongri-type jars were first identified in a cave at Misong-ri in Uiju. They have flat bottoms, rounded bodies, spreading rims and strap-like handles. Many examples come from stone-coffin burials, helping archaeologists compare communities across Liaoning, Jilin and northern Korea.

Some northwestern pots look rather like flowerpots, but soot on their outer surfaces suggests they were used to boil food. The National Museum of Korea connects this pottery with the Daedong River region. Ancient cooking can leave a stubborn black trace long after the meal has vanished.

A study of Bronze Age plant remains in Liaoning and Jilin identifies rice, foxtail millet and broomcorn millet. These regional findings help reconstruct Gojoseon’s wider food world. Access to evidence from northern Korea is uneven, so they cannot supply one menu for the whole kingdom.

Animal remains in the same regional study point to cattle, pigs and dogs being raised, with fewer sheep. Farming households combined crop growing with animal care. The evidence describes a varied working landscape rather than a population living entirely by hunting.

Coastal communities around Bohai Bay caught fish and gathered shellfish, while inland communities used rivers. Storage pits held surplus food. Catching or growing enough to eat was only part of the job: households also had to keep some of it for later.

sections.title: Later society, families and political power

items.text: In the later Wiman phase, beginning in the second century BCE, officials came from both established local groups and immigrant communities. Song Ho Jung interprets the government as a coalition in which regional leaders retained influence. The king had to work with other powerful people.

Wiman Joseon benefited from controlling exchanges between Han China and smaller neighbouring states. Its position made trade a political resource: deciding who could pass through or deal directly with another power could strengthen the court. These ambitions also contributed to conflict with Han.

The later Hanshu preserves three rules traditionally associated with Gojoseon: killing, injury and theft brought severe penalties. Theft could lead to enslavement in the injured household. These rules reveal inequality and protection of property, but they do not prove that enslaved labour dominated the economy.

The Hanshu also claims that a person punished for theft could face difficulty finding a marriage partner even after paying for release. This is an external author’s account of shame and social reputation, offering a narrow glimpse of family expectations rather than a complete description of marriage.

After the conquest, a household register dated 45 BCE from a tomb at Jeongbaek-dong in Pyongyang records the population of Lelang. It provides evidence for local communities continuing under new administration. A kingdom’s defeat did not make its inhabitants disappear.

sections.title: A written account from outside Gojoseon

items.text: Classical Chinese: “相傷以穀償”, meaning “Compensate injury with grain.” The phrase survives in the later Han-dynasty history Hanshu’s account of Joseon people. It is external written testimony, not an inscription produced by a Gojoseon scribe. No securely identified local-language sentence was established in the sources used for this card.

ending.text: Han armies conquered Wiman Joseon in 108 BCE after a prolonged campaign and internal divisions. Han established commanderies in the former kingdom’s territory, while local communities continued. The imported map endpoint of 323 BCE is much earlier and is not Gojoseon’s fall; later Korean states developed from a changing regional landscape.
